claims.text: Increasing Al content in near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys enhances short-range chemical ordering.
Increasing Al content promotes B2 phase formation.
Al-enhanced short-range ordering stabilizes the phase balance.
The stabilized phase balance preserves high-temperature strength.
The stabilized phase balance preserves environmental resistance.
The stabilized phase balance preserves radiation tolerance.
The stabilized phase balance preserves cryogenic toughness.
The initial near-equiatomic alloy is predominantly disordered FCC.
The initial alloy contains a minor, dispersed B2-ordered constituent.
Increasing Al while reducing Ni increases the fraction of locally ordered B2 regions.
Increasing Al while reducing Ni improves the distribution of locally ordered B2 regions.
Local ordering interactions between Al and Ni favor formation of an ordered B2 phase.
Local ordering lowers the free energy relative to the disordered FCC state.
The reduction in free energy stabilizes the overall phase mixture.
Ordered regions impede defect motion under extreme-environment exposure.
Ordered regions impede grain-boundary degradation under extreme-environment exposure.
The Al-enriched alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in B2 ordering relative to the baseline.
The Al-enriched alloy will have comparable or improved high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies within approximately ±5–10 at.% variations of key elements around equiatomic composition.
Compositional deviations beyond the stated window may produce additional phase-formation mechanisms.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows property performance to remain merely comparable to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule says that absence of anticipated improvements falsifies the hypothesis. Thus, comparable performance is simultaneously permitted by the prediction and potentially treated as falsifying.
